intro: You already know which words are strong in a short sentence and how to clap the English beat. Now you take that beat into longer sentences and add the melody: how your voice goes up ↗ or down ↘ in lists, questions and question tags, and how it shows feelings like surprise, interest and annoyance. Say every example out loud, and exaggerate a little!
teachingNotes: Builds on a2-pron-stress-linking (content words strong, function words weak, linking, counting beats in short sentences) and b1-indirect-questions-tags (how to build a tag). Recap in a line; don't re-teach. New here: stress-timed rhythm in LONGER sentences. Adding weak words doesn't add beats, it makes the weak words faster (RI-na SENT the E-mails = 3; RI-na has SENT the E-mails to her BOSS = 4). Helper verbs (has, have, will, can, is, do) are weak when they only help; negative helpers (can't, don't, didn't) are strong; a helper at the end or in a short answer is said in full (Yes, she HAS). Weak forms with a short 'uh' (like the e in Indonesian sedang): to 'tuh', for 'fuh', of 'uhv', and 'uhn', can 'kuhn'. Beat count = number of content words, one beat on each word's stressed syllable (MAN-a-ger, Ja-KAR-ta). Common error: every syllable the same length and strength, as in Indonesian; right: I WANT to GO to the SHOP. Checkpoint beat items avoid ambiguous words (compounds, very/really, this/that, phrasal-verb particles).

Intonation = the melody of the voice, described with arrows (↗ up, ↘ down, → flat) and plain Indonesian (nada naik / nada turun). No IPA and no tone-unit theory (no 'tonic syllable', no fall-rise). Present the patterns as tendencies, not laws: statements usually fall; wh-questions (what, where, when, who, why, how) usually fall; yes/no questions usually rise; lists rise on every item and fall on the last one (apples ↗, bananas ↗ and oranges ↘), and phone numbers in groups work the same way (0812 ↗ 5567 ↗ 3490 ↘). Trap: 'question = voice up' for every question; a rising wh-question can sound unsure or like asking someone to repeat.

Question tags: voice DOWN on the tag ↘ = you're sure and just want agreement (small talk, things you can both see: It's hot today, isn't it? ↘). Voice UP ↗ = a real question, you're not sure (The meeting's at ten, isn't it? ↗). Node common error: a rising tag when you expect agreement. Test it with situations (does the speaker already know?) and text answers (up/down, sure/not sure). If the learner makes a form error (isn't it after every sentence), correct it in one line with the rule from b1-indirect-questions-tags.

Emotion: English uses a wider pitch range than Indonesian. Surprise = a big jump from low to very high (Really?! ↗); interest = the voice moves and starts higher; boredom = flat and low (→); annoyance = slow, low, strong fall on the key word (Not again! ↘), and sarcasm = a positive word said low and falling (Oh, perfect. ↘ when the printer breaks). Indonesian trap and node common error: a flat Indonesian-style melody makes English Really. or Thank you. sound bored, cold or rude; encourage learners to exaggerate when practising. Also: Sorry? ↗ = please say it again; Sorry. ↘ = an apology.

Audio limits: every recording in this lesson is read once, naturally, by one voice. It doesn't demonstrate exaggerated or emotional intonation or both tunes of a tag. So listening questions only test rhythm, stress and meaning that a natural reading gives (count the beats, pick the stressed word, what was said). Test intonation knowledge in text: which arrow, which meaning, which feeling. If the learner asks to hear the difference, describe it (start low, jump high; flat and low) and ask them to say it aloud.

Grammar scope: A0–A2 grammar (present simple/continuous, past simple, present perfect with just/already/yet, will, going to, can/should/have to) plus indirect questions and question tags. No passive, past perfect, second conditional, reported speech or relative clauses in examples. Don't teach contrastive stress (moving stress to change meaning) or fall-rise tones. British and American speakers use the same basic patterns; the exact melody varies by speaker and region (centre/center, lift/elevator).

keyPoints.title: Keep the beat in longer sentences
keyPoints.explanation: English is stress-timed: the strong words (content words) come at roughly regular beats, and the weak words between them are squeezed. Adding weak words doesn't add beats; it makes the weak words faster and shorter ('tuh', 'kuhn'). Helper verbs like has, can and will are weak; can't and don't are strong. One beat per content word.

examples.en: Rina has sent the emails to her boss.
examples.id: Rina sudah mengirim email-emailnya ke atasannya. (4 ketukan: RI-na SENT E-mails BOSS)

examples.en: Dimas works for a bank in the centre of Bandung.
examples.id: Dimas bekerja di sebuah bank di pusat kota Bandung. (5 ketukan: DI-mas WORKS BANK CEN-tre BAN-dung)

id.title: Jaga ketukan di kalimat yang lebih panjang
id.explanation: Bahasa Inggris itu stress-timed: kata-kata kuat (kata isi) datang dengan ketukan yang kurang lebih teratur, dan kata-kata lemah di antaranya diselipkan. Menambah kata lemah tidak menambah ketukan; kata lemahnya justru jadi lebih cepat dan pendek ('te', 'ken'). Kata kerja bantu seperti has, can dan will lemah; can't dan don't kuat. Satu ketukan untuk setiap kata isi.

keyPoints.title: Up or down: lists, questions and tags
keyPoints.explanation: In a list the voice goes up on each item and down on the last one. Statements and wh-questions usually go down; yes/no questions usually go up. A question tag goes down when you're sure and want agreement, and up when you really don't know.

examples.en: We need apples, bananas and oranges.
examples.id: Kita perlu apel, pisang dan jeruk. (apples ↗, bananas ↗ and oranges ↘)
Panas ya hari ini? (↘ kamu yakin dan cuma minta persetujuan)

id.title: Naik atau turun: daftar, pertanyaan dan tag
id.explanation: Dalam daftar, suara naik di setiap item dan turun di item terakhir. Kalimat biasa dan pertanyaan dengan kata tanya (wh-question) biasanya turun; pertanyaan ya/tidak biasanya naik. Question tag turun kalau kamu yakin dan ingin lawan bicara setuju, dan naik kalau kamu benar-benar tidak tahu.

keyPoints.title: Show feelings with a wider range
keyPoints.explanation: English moves the voice more than Indonesian. A big jump up shows surprise, a moving voice shows interest, flat and low sounds bored, and a slow, low, strong fall shows annoyance. A flat 'Really.' can sound bored or rude, so make your voice move.

examples.id: Masa? Keren banget! (terkejut: lompatan nada besar ↗)

id.title: Tunjukkan perasaan dengan rentang nada yang lebar
id.explanation: Bahasa Inggris menggerakkan suara lebih banyak daripada bahasa Indonesia. Lompatan naik yang besar menunjukkan terkejut, suara yang bergerak menunjukkan tertarik, datar dan rendah terdengar bosan, dan turun yang pelan, rendah dan kuat menunjukkan kesal. 'Really.' yang datar bisa terdengar bosan atau tidak sopan, jadi gerakkan suaramu.

guidedPractice.prompt: How many strong beats are in 'The children are playing in the garden'? Write the number.
guidedPractice.hint: Count only the content words: CHIL-dren, PLAY-ing, GAR-den. the, are and in are squeezed between the beats.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a list, does your voice usually go up or down on each item before the last one? Write up or down.
guidedPractice.hint: Up tells the listener 'there's more coming'. Only the last item goes down.

guidedPractice.prompt: Does a wh-question like 'What time does the bank open?' usually go up or down at the end? Write up or down.
guidedPractice.hint: The question word (what time) already shows it's a question, so the voice can go down like a statement.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your friend is telling you some news. To sound interested, should your voice move up and down a lot or stay flat? Write move or flat.
guidedPractice.hint: In English a wide range sounds interested and friendly. Flat and low sounds bored.

independentPractice.prompt: Write the stressed words (the content words) in: 'Rina has finished the report for her boss.'
independentPractice.hint: has is a helper here, so it's weak. the, for and her are function words.

independentPractice.prompt: Dimas asks a new colleague: 'You're from Medan, aren't you?' His voice goes up ↗ on the tag. Is he sure or not sure? Write sure or not sure.
independentPractice.hint: Up on the tag = a real question. Down = you're sure and want agreement.

independentPractice.prompt: Someone says 'Sorry?' with the voice going up ↗. Do they want to apologise, or do they want you to repeat? Write apologise or repeat.
independentPractice.hint: Sorry? ↗ means 'What did you say?'. Sorry. ↘ is an apology.

assessment.prompt: How many strong beats are in this sentence? 'Rina sent the photos to her manager on Monday.' Write the number.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 5 (RI-na, SENT, PHO-tos, MAN-a-ger, MON-day; the, to, her and on are weak and squeezed in). 9 (every word) = 0. 4 or 6 = 30 (close, but a content word is missed or a function word is counted).

assessment.prompt: Listen. How many strong beats (content words) do you hear? Write the number.
assessment.listen: Dimas is waiting for the train at the station.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 4 (DI-mas, WAIT-ing, TRAIN, STA-tion; is, for, the, at, the are squeezed in). 9 (every word) = 0. 3 or 5 = 30.

assessment.prompt: Rina reads her shopping list to Budi: 'We need rice, eggs, cooking oil and sugar.' On which item does her voice go down ↘? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: sugar (the last item goes down to show the list is finished; rice, eggs and cooking oil go up). 'rice' = 0 (the first item goes up: more is coming). 'cooking oil' or 'eggs' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan and a colleague are looking out of the office window at heavy rain. He says: 'It's raining again, isn't it?' He can see the rain and just wants his colleague to agree. Does his voice go up or down on 'isn't it'? Write up or down.
assessment.rubric: Correct: down (he's sure, so it isn't a real question: a falling tag invites agreement). 'up' = 0 (a rising tag would mean he really doubts it's raining: the error this lesson targets).

assessment.prompt: Sari thinks the deadline for the sales report is Friday, but she isn't sure and really wants to check. She asks her manager: 'The deadline is Friday, isn't it?' Does her voice go up or down on 'isn't it'? Write up or down.
assessment.rubric: Correct: up (she isn't sure, so it's a real question: rising tag). 'down' = 0 (a falling tag means she's sure and only wants agreement).

assessment.prompt: Budi tells you happily: 'I passed my driving test!' You answer 'Wow.' in a flat, low voice that hardly moves. How does that sound to Budi? Write interested or bored.
assessment.rubric: Correct: bored (a flat, low voice with no movement sounds bored or even rude in English, whatever the word; to sound interested, the voice jumps up: Wow! ↗). 'interested' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani's laptop crashes for the third time this morning. She says 'Oh, great.' slowly, in a low voice that falls at the end. What does she really feel? Write surprised, interested or annoyed.
assessment.rubric: Correct: annoyed (great is a positive word, but a slow, low, falling voice says the opposite: she's annoyed, this is sarcasm). 'angry' = 70 (close, but annoyed is the feeling asked for). 'surprised' or 'interested' = 0 (those need a voice that jumps up).

blocks.text:
Quick recap: **content words** (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, question words, *not*) are strong; **function words** (*a, the, to, of, in, at, and, is, I, my*) are weak. English is **stress-timed**: the timing follows the **stressed** (strong) words, which come at roughly regular beats. Indonesian is closer to **syllable-timed**: every syllable gets about the same time (*sa-ya-mau-ke-pa-sar*).

Now the sentences get longer. Add words, and watch the beats:
- *RI-na SENT the E-mails.* (3 beats)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails.* (still 3: *has* only helps, so it's weak)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails to her BOSS.* (4 beats)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails to her BOSS in Ja-KAR-ta.* (5 beats)

The more weak syllables there are between two beats, the **faster** you say them. *to her* between *E-mails* and *BOSS* is very quick and quiet.

**Helper verbs are weak, main verbs are strong.** *has, have, is, are, will, can, do, does* are usually weak when they only help another verb: *RI-na has SENT…*, *we can MEET…*. Two exceptions: a **negative** helper is strong (*I CAN'T COME*, *she DIDN'T CALL*), and a helper at the **end** of a sentence or in a short answer is said in full (*Yes, she HAS.*).

**Weak sounds.** Many function words lose their full vowel and use a short, weak 'uh', like the *e* in Indonesian *sedang*: *to* → 'tuh', *for* → 'fuh', *of* → 'uhv', *and* → 'uhn', *can* → 'kuhn'. That's how they fit between the beats.

**The Indonesian trap:** giving every syllable the same time and strength. In a long sentence that sounds slow and robotic, and the important words get lost.

**How to count beats:** find the content words; each one is **one** beat, on its stressed syllable (*MAN-a-ger*, *Ja-KAR-ta*). Then clap.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: **kata isi** (kata benda, kata kerja utama, kata sifat, kata tanya, *not*) itu kuat; **kata tugas** (*a, the, to, of, in, at, and, is, I, my*) itu lemah. Bahasa Inggris itu **stress-timed** (ritmenya mengikuti tekanan): waktunya mengikuti kata-kata yang **ditekan** (kuat), yang datang dengan ketukan kurang lebih teratur. Bahasa Indonesia lebih dekat ke **syllable-timed** (ritmenya mengikuti suku kata): setiap suku kata mendapat waktu yang kira-kira sama (*sa-ya-mau-ke-pa-sar*).

Sekarang kalimatnya makin panjang. Tambahkan kata, dan perhatikan ketukannya:
- *RI-na SENT the E-mails.* (3 ketukan)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails.* (tetap 3: *has* cuma membantu, jadi lemah)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails to her BOSS.* (4 ketukan)
- *RI-na has SENT the E-mails to her BOSS in Ja-KAR-ta.* (5 ketukan)

Makin banyak suku kata lemah di antara dua ketukan, makin **cepat** kamu mengucapkannya. *to her* di antara *E-mails* dan *BOSS* diucapkan sangat cepat dan pelan.

**Kata kerja bantu lemah, kata kerja utama kuat.** *has, have, is, are, will, can, do, does* biasanya lemah kalau cuma membantu kata kerja lain: *RI-na has SENT…*, *we can MEET…*. Dua pengecualian: kata kerja bantu **negatif** itu kuat (*I CAN'T COME*, *she DIDN'T CALL*), dan kata kerja bantu di **akhir** kalimat atau di jawaban pendek diucapkan utuh (*Yes, she HAS.*).

**Bunyi lemah.** Banyak kata tugas kehilangan vokal penuhnya dan memakai bunyi pendek yang lemah, seperti **e** di kata *sedang* (bukan é seperti di *sate*): *to* → 'te', *for* → 'fe', *of* → 'ev', *and* → 'en', *can* → 'ken'. Begitulah kata-kata ini muat di antara ketukan.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** memberi setiap suku kata waktu dan kekuatan yang sama. Di kalimat panjang, itu terdengar lambat dan seperti robot, dan kata-kata pentingnya hilang.

**Cara menghitung ketukan:** cari kata isinya; setiap kata isi = **satu** ketukan, di suku kata yang ditekan (*MAN-a-ger*, *Ja-KAR-ta*). Lalu tepuk tangan.

rows.id: Rina sudah mengirim email-emailnya ke atasannya.

I can't find my phone in the kitchen.

blocks.text: Tap the table on each strong word. Start slowly and keep the taps even, then go faster: the weak words have to fit between the taps. A long sentence? Say it in small groups of words, with a short pause where you'd write a comma.

id.text: Ketuk meja di setiap kata kuat. Mulai pelan-pelan dan jaga ketukannya tetap rata, lalu percepat: kata-kata lemahnya harus muat di antara ketukan. Kalimatnya panjang? Ucapkan per kelompok kata kecil, dengan jeda singkat di tempat kamu akan menulis koma.

blocks.prompt: How many strong beats are in 'Sari is talking to the new students'?
blocks.explain: The content words are SA-ri, TALK-ing, NEW and STU-dents: 4 beats. is, to and the are squeezed in. 7 would mean every word is strong, the Indonesian habit.

id.prompt: Berapa ketukan kuat di 'Sari is talking to the new students'?
id.explain: Kata isinya SA-ri, TALK-ing, NEW dan STU-dents: 4 ketukan. is, to dan the diselipkan. 7 berarti semua kata kuat, kebiasaan dari bahasa Indonesia.

id.title: Ketukan di kalimat yang lebih panjang

blocks.text:
**Intonation** is the melody of your voice: how it goes **up** (↗) or **down** (↘), mostly on the last strong word of the sentence. Stress tells people *which* words matter. Intonation tells them *what you mean*: Are you finished? Are you asking? Are you sure? How do you feel?

The basic patterns (they are what usually happens, not strict laws: people vary):
- **Statements** usually go **down** at the end: *I work in Ja-KAR-ta. ↘* Down = 'I've finished.'
- **Wh-questions** (with *what, where, when, who, why, how*) usually go **down** too: *Where do you WORK? ↘* The question word already shows it's a question.
- **Yes/no questions** (you answer them with yes or no) usually go **up**: *Do you work in Ja-KAR-ta? ↗* Just like Indonesian *Kamu kerja di Jakarta? ↗*
- **Lists** go **up** on every item and **down** on the last one: *We need AP-ples ↗, ba-NA-nas ↗ and OR-anges ↘.* Up = 'there's more coming'. Down = 'that's the end'.

**The trap:** thinking 'question = voice up' every time. A wh-question with the voice going up (*Where do you work? ↗*) can sound unsure, or as if you want the person to say it again. And in a list, if every item goes down, the listener thinks you've finished after the first one.

id.text:
**Intonasi** adalah melodi suaramu: bagaimana suara **naik** (↗, nada naik) atau **turun** (↘, nada turun), terutama di kata kuat terakhir dalam kalimat. Tekanan memberi tahu orang kata *mana* yang penting. Intonasi memberi tahu mereka *apa maksudmu*: Kamu sudah selesai? Kamu bertanya? Kamu yakin? Bagaimana perasaanmu?

Pola dasarnya (ini yang biasanya terjadi, bukan hukum yang kaku: setiap orang bisa berbeda):
- **Kalimat biasa** (pernyataan) biasanya **turun** di akhir: *I work in Ja-KAR-ta. ↘* Turun = 'Saya sudah selesai bicara.'
- **Wh-question** (pertanyaan dengan *what, where, when, who, why, how*) biasanya juga **turun**: *Where do you WORK? ↘* Kata tanyanya sudah menunjukkan bahwa itu pertanyaan.
- **Pertanyaan ya/tidak** (dijawab dengan yes atau no) biasanya **naik**: *Do you work in Ja-KAR-ta? ↗* Sama seperti *Kamu kerja di Jakarta? ↗* dalam bahasa Indonesia.
- **Daftar** naik di setiap item dan **turun** di item terakhir: *We need AP-ples ↗, ba-NA-nas ↗ and OR-anges ↘.* Naik = 'masih ada lagi'. Turun = 'sudah, itu saja'.

**Jebakannya:** mengira 'pertanyaan = suara naik' setiap saat. Wh-question dengan suara naik (*Where do you work? ↗*) bisa terdengar ragu, atau seperti kamu minta orangnya mengulang. Dan dalam daftar, kalau setiap item turun, pendengar mengira kamu sudah selesai sesudah item pertama.

rows.en: What time does the meeting start?
I bought rice, eggs and cooking oil.
rows.id: Saya beli beras, telur dan minyak goreng.
rows.note: list: rice ↗, eggs ↗ and cooking oil ↘

id.note: daftar: rice ↗, eggs ↗ and cooking oil ↘

rows.en: We can meet on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday.
rows.id: Kita bisa ketemu hari Senin, Selasa atau Kamis.
rows.note: list with or: Monday ↗, Tuesday ↗ or Thursday ↘

id.note: daftar dengan or: Monday ↗, Tuesday ↗ or Thursday ↘

blocks.text: Phone numbers work like a list. Say them in groups, up at the end of each group and down at the end: *0812 ↗ 5567 ↗ 3490 ↘*. The rise tells the listener 'wait, there's more', so they don't stop writing.

id.text: Nomor telepon bekerja seperti daftar. Ucapkan per kelompok, naik di akhir setiap kelompok dan turun di bagian paling akhir: *0812 ↗ 5567 ↗ 3490 ↘*. Nada naik memberi tahu pendengar 'tunggu, masih ada lagi', jadi mereka tidak berhenti menulis.

blocks.prompt: Which question usually goes down ↘ at the end?
blocks.explain: Where do you live? is a wh-question (it starts with where), so the voice usually goes down. The other two are yes/no questions, so they usually go up.

id.prompt: Pertanyaan mana yang biasanya turun ↘ di akhir?
id.explain: Where do you live? adalah wh-question (diawali where), jadi suaranya biasanya turun. Dua lainnya pertanyaan ya/tidak, jadi biasanya naik.

material.title: Question tags: sure ↘ or really asking ↗

blocks.text:
You know how to build a question tag: *It's hot today, **isn't it**?* (the helper verb, flipped, plus a pronoun). Now the voice. The **same words** can mean two different things:
- **Voice down on the tag ↘**: you're **sure**, and you just want the other person to **agree**. It isn't a real question. Use it in small talk and for things you can both see: *It's HOT to-DAY, ISN'T it? ↘* (→ 'Yes, terrible!')
- **Voice up on the tag ↗**: you're **not sure**, and you **really want to know**. It's a real question: *The MEET-ing's at TEN, ISN'T it? ↗* (→ 'Hmm, I think it's at eleven.')

**The trap:** 'It's a question, so my voice goes up.' Many learners raise every tag. But if you raise the tag on *It's hot, isn't it?* while you're both sweating in the sun, it sounds strange, as if you really doubt that it's hot. When you expect the other person to agree, go **down**.

It works the same after a negative sentence: *You don't eat MEAT, DO you? ↘* (I'm quite sure you don't) or *↗* (I really don't know).

id.text:
Kamu sudah tahu cara membuat question tag: *It's hot today, **isn't it**?* (kata kerja bantu, dibalik, ditambah kata ganti). Sekarang suaranya. **Kata-kata yang sama** bisa punya dua arti berbeda:
- **Suara turun di tag ↘**: kamu **yakin**, dan kamu cuma ingin lawan bicara **setuju**. Ini bukan pertanyaan sungguhan. Pakai untuk basa-basi dan untuk hal yang sama-sama kalian lihat: *It's HOT to-DAY, ISN'T it? ↘* (→ 'Iya, parah!')
- **Suara naik di tag ↗**: kamu **tidak yakin**, dan kamu **benar-benar ingin tahu**. Ini pertanyaan sungguhan: *The MEET-ing's at TEN, ISN'T it? ↗* (→ 'Hmm, kayaknya jam sebelas.')

**Jebakannya:** 'Ini pertanyaan, jadi suaraku naik.' Banyak pelajar menaikkan setiap tag. Tapi kalau kamu menaikkan tag di *It's hot, isn't it?* padahal kalian berdua sedang kepanasan di bawah matahari, itu terdengar aneh, seolah kamu benar-benar ragu apakah cuacanya panas. Kalau kamu berharap lawan bicara setuju, **turunkan** suaramu.

Sama juga sesudah kalimat negatif: *You don't eat MEAT, DO you? ↘* (aku cukup yakin kamu tidak makan daging) atau *↗* (aku benar-benar tidak tahu).

rows.en: It's really hot today, isn't it?
The train leaves at seven, doesn't it?
rows.note: ↗ if you're not sure and want to check

id.note: ↗ kalau kamu tidak yakin dan ingin memastikan

rows.note: ↘ if you're almost sure; ↗ if you really don't know

id.note: ↘ kalau kamu hampir yakin; ↗ kalau kamu benar-benar tidak tahu

rows.en: Pak Hasan didn't call, did he?
rows.note: ↗ a real question: you want to know

blocks.text: Not sure which one? Ask yourself: do I already know the answer? **Yes** → down ↘. **No** → up ↗. A falling tag does the job of a friendly Indonesian *…ya?* when you just want agreement (*Panas banget, ya?*). A rising tag is closer to *…kan? Bener nggak?* when you really check.

id.text: Bingung pilih yang mana? Tanya dirimu: apakah aku sudah tahu jawabannya? **Ya** → turun ↘. **Tidak** → naik ↗. Tag yang turun punya fungsi seperti *…ya?* yang ramah dalam bahasa Indonesia, saat kamu cuma ingin persetujuan (*Panas banget, ya?*). Tag yang naik lebih mirip *…kan? Bener nggak?* saat kamu benar-benar memastikan.

blocks.prompt: Your colleague is sure the office closes at five, and she wants you to agree. Which one sounds right?
options: The office closes at five, doesn't it? ↘
The office closes at five, doesn't it? ↗
The office closes at five, isn't it? ↘
blocks.explain: She's sure and wants agreement, so the tag goes down ↘. Up ↗ would mean she really doesn't know. isn't it is the wrong tag: closes has no helper, so the tag uses does → doesn't it.

id.prompt: Rekan kerjamu yakin kantornya tutup jam lima, dan dia ingin kamu setuju. Mana yang terdengar benar?
id.explain: Dia yakin dan ingin kamu setuju, jadi tag-nya turun ↘. Naik ↗ berarti dia benar-benar tidak tahu. isn't it adalah tag yang salah: closes tidak punya kata kerja bantu, jadi tag-nya memakai does → doesn't it.

id.title: Question tag: yakin ↘ atau benar-benar bertanya ↗

blocks.text:
English uses a **wide pitch range** to show feelings. (**Pitch range** = how far your voice travels from low to high.) A voice that moves a lot sounds **interested** and **friendly**. A voice that hardly moves sounds **bored**, **cold** or even **rude**.
- **Surprise**: a big jump up, from low to very high: *REAL-ly?! ↗* *You GOT the JOB?! ↗*
- **Interest**: the voice moves and starts a bit higher: *Oh, REAL-ly? ↗ What HAP-pened? ↘*
- **Boredom**: flat and low, almost no movement (→): *Oh. That's nice. →* It says 'I don't care.'
- **Annoyance** (feeling irritated): slow and low, with a strong fall on the key word: *Not a-GAIN! ↘* People sometimes even say a **positive** word in a low, slow, falling voice to show they're annoyed: *Oh, PER-fect. ↘* when the printer breaks again. The word is positive, but the voice says the opposite. This is called **sarcasm**.

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian is usually spoken with a **flatter** melody: the voice moves up and down less. That sounds normal in Indonesian, but in English the same flat voice sends a message you don't mean. A flat *Really.* → sounds **bored** or even **rude**, and a flat *Thank you.* → sounds cold. So when you want to sound interested or friendly, let your voice move **more** than feels natural: start higher and let it go up and down.

id.text:
Bahasa Inggris memakai **rentang nada yang lebar** untuk menunjukkan perasaan. (**Rentang nada** = seberapa jauh suaramu bergerak dari rendah ke tinggi.) Suara yang banyak bergerak terdengar **tertarik** dan **ramah**. Suara yang hampir tidak bergerak terdengar **bosan**, **dingin**, atau bahkan **tidak sopan**.
- **Terkejut**: lompatan naik yang besar, dari rendah ke sangat tinggi: *REAL-ly?! ↗* *You GOT the JOB?! ↗*
- **Tertarik**: suaranya bergerak dan mulai sedikit lebih tinggi: *Oh, REAL-ly? ↗ What HAP-pened? ↘*
- **Bosan**: datar dan rendah, hampir tidak bergerak (→): *Oh. That's nice. →* Artinya 'aku nggak peduli.'
- **Kesal**: pelan dan rendah, dengan nada turun yang kuat di kata kuncinya: *Not a-GAIN! ↘* Kadang orang bahkan mengucapkan kata yang **positif** dengan suara rendah, pelan dan turun untuk menunjukkan kesal: *Oh, PER-fect. ↘* saat printernya rusak lagi. Katanya positif, tapi suaranya bilang sebaliknya. Ini disebut **sarkasme** (sindiran).

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia biasanya diucapkan dengan melodi yang **lebih datar**: suaranya lebih sedikit naik-turun. Itu terdengar normal dalam bahasa Indonesia, tapi dalam bahasa Inggris suara datar yang sama mengirim pesan yang tidak kamu maksud. *Really.* yang datar → terdengar **bosan** atau bahkan **tidak sopan**, dan *Thank you.* yang datar → terdengar dingin. Jadi kalau kamu ingin terdengar tertarik atau ramah, biarkan suaramu bergerak **lebih banyak** dari yang terasa wajar: mulai lebih tinggi dan biarkan naik-turun.

blocks.text: One word, two meanings: *Sorry? ↗* = 'What did you say?' (please say it again). *Sorry. ↘* = an apology (*maaf*). Practise in front of a mirror and exaggerate: at the start, too much melody is better than too little.

id.text: Satu kata, dua arti: *Sorry? ↗* = 'Tadi bilang apa?' (tolong ulangi). *Sorry. ↘* = permintaan maaf. Berlatihlah di depan cermin dan lebih-lebihkan: di awal, melodi yang terlalu banyak lebih baik daripada terlalu sedikit.

blocks.prompt: Rina's friend shows her some wedding photos. Rina says 'That's nice.' in a flat, low voice →. How does it sound?
blocks.explain: A flat, low voice with no movement sounds bored, even when the words are positive. Excited and surprised need a voice that jumps up and moves a lot.

id.prompt: Teman Rina menunjukkan foto-foto pernikahan. Rina bilang 'That's nice.' dengan suara datar dan rendah →. Bagaimana kedengarannya?
id.explain: Suara datar dan rendah tanpa gerakan terdengar bosan, walaupun kata-katanya positif. Senang sekali dan terkejut butuh suara yang melompat naik dan banyak bergerak.

suggestedQuestions: Why does English sound so fast when the small words are squeezed?
When does a question go up and when does it go down?
How do I know if a question tag should go up or down?
How can I sound more interested without sounding fake?

resources.title: Question tags
resources.note: A B1–B2 grammar page with two short quizzes. The part on intonation explains falling tags (you're sure the listener will agree) and rising tags (you're less sure). The rest reviews how to build tags. There's no audio, so practise both tunes out loud yourself.

id.note: Halaman tata bahasa level B1–B2 dengan dua kuis pendek. Bagian tentang intonasi menjelaskan tag yang turun (kamu yakin pendengar akan setuju) dan tag yang naik (kamu kurang yakin). Sisanya mengulang cara membuat tag. Tidak ada audionya, jadi latih kedua nada itu sendiri dengan suara keras.

id.intro: Kamu sudah tahu kata mana yang kuat di kalimat pendek dan cara bertepuk tangan mengikuti ketukan bahasa Inggris. Sekarang kamu membawa ketukan itu ke kalimat yang lebih panjang dan menambahkan melodinya: kapan suaramu naik ↗ atau turun ↘ dalam daftar, pertanyaan dan question tag, dan bagaimana suaramu menunjukkan perasaan seperti terkejut, tertarik dan kesal. Ucapkan setiap contoh dengan suara keras, dan sedikit lebih-lebihkan!
suggestedQuestions: Kenapa bahasa Inggris terdengar cepat sekali kalau kata-kata kecilnya diselipkan?
Kapan pertanyaan naik dan kapan turun?
Bagaimana aku tahu question tag harus naik atau turun?
Bagaimana caranya terdengar lebih tertarik tanpa terdengar dibuat-buat?

assessment.ri-1: Berapa ketukan kuat di kalimat ini? 'Rina sent the photos to her manager on Monday.' Tulis angkanya.
assessment.ri-2: Dengarkan. Berapa ketukan kuat (kata isi) yang kamu dengar? Tulis angkanya.
assessment.ri-3: Rina membacakan daftar belanjanya ke Budi: 'We need rice, eggs, cooking oil and sugar.' Di item mana suaranya turun ↘? Tulis katanya.
assessment.ri-4: Pak Hasan dan rekan kerjanya sedang melihat hujan deras dari jendela kantor. Dia bilang: 'It's raining again, isn't it?' Dia bisa melihat hujannya dan cuma ingin rekannya setuju. Apakah suaranya naik atau turun di 'isn't it'? Tulis up atau down.
assessment.ri-5: Sari mengira tenggat laporan penjualan hari Jumat, tapi dia tidak yakin dan benar-benar ingin memastikan. Dia bertanya ke manajernya: 'The deadline is Friday, isn't it?' Apakah suaranya naik atau turun di 'isn't it'? Tulis up atau down.
assessment.ri-6: Budi bercerita dengan senang: 'I passed my driving test!' Kamu menjawab 'Wow.' dengan suara datar dan rendah yang hampir tidak bergerak. Bagaimana kedengarannya bagi Budi? Tulis interested atau bored.
assessment.ri-7: Laptop Bu Ani mati mendadak untuk ketiga kalinya pagi ini. Dia bilang 'Oh, great.' pelan-pelan, dengan suara rendah yang turun di akhir. Apa yang sebenarnya dia rasakan? Tulis surprised, interested atau annoyed.
